scenario: AITA in relation to my GF's attempt to lose weight? | I've been dating my GF for 3 years. She's upset at her current weight. She's put on about 100lbs since we started dating. I've never mentioned it because she has bipolar disorder, and as I struggle with depression I fully understand how food can take the edge off when you get seriously overwhelmed with depression. But for health reasons and of course other reasons, of course I would like for her to get back to a healthy weight. My girlfriend's bipolar disorder has been a challenge for me, as where I would normally be assertive in a relationship on issues - I often have to back down in arguments because she responds poorly to being challenged. I often feel like I'm walking on ice, but I do my best to try understand her and work at helping her and supporting her as best I can. She is not happy with her current weight, and constantly remarks about it and has been complaining about it for over a year without doing anything about it. I tell her we can work on it together as a team, and both fix our diet. I feel this is the best way to go about it, rather than telling her that SHE needs to lose weight. I don't want her feeling like I'm initiating it, or that it's a journey she needs to take alone. Or that I'm pushing her to do it. For it to be a healthy journey, it needs to be something she is motivated to do and if I do it with her, then it doesn't feel like it's all on her. So, last week she decided to work on her diet. She was upset today because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I told her to not worry about the short term results - that it had only been a week, but to focus on months down the line to see changes. She was extremely defeatist and said she'll never lose weight. This kinda irritated me, because it had only been a week since she started. I felt like she hadn't fully committed, because she was drinking soft drinks and eating chips which are high in carbs so I brought that up, if she wants to see results quicker - that cutting out the junk food completely (rather than cutting down) will help her. Now I understand she's trying to make a change, but the defeatist attitude after only a week is difficult to work with. She then got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight". To which I replied that I wasn't, I had never in our entire relationship brought up her weight, and was just discussing her diet and how she was eating and drinking things that will make her progress slower. She then told me to drop it and leave it alone, and is now in a huff with me for the past few hours over it. I understand this is the nature of her bipolar disorder, and she will shut down anything she's challenged about something. Am I the asshole for challenging her defeatist attitude on her results, when she was taking short-cuts with junk food?

Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) The Core Issue: You’re Not the Asshole (But You’re Not Perfect Either)** **Why you’re *not* the asshole:** - You’ve been **supportive** for 3 years without judgment, which is **rare and admirable**, especially given her bipolar disorder and your own depression. - You’re **not demanding** she lose weight—you’re framing it as a **shared goal** ("we can work on it together"), which reduces pressure. - You’re **aware of her mental health** and trying to navigate this delicately, which shows maturity. **Why you’re *not off the hook*:** - **Timing and delivery matter.** Even if your intent was good, your **tone and phrasing** escalated the conflict. Here’s how it went wrong: - **Minimizing her feelings:** You said, *"Don’t worry about short-term results—focus on months down the line."* While true, this **dismissed her immediate frustration**, which made her feel invalidated. - **Criticizing her choices:** Calling out her junk food consumption ("*cutting out completely*") came across as **condescending** ("*she’s not fully committed*"). Even if you meant it as advice, it sounded like **judgment**. - **Defensiveness:** When she got angry, you **double-downed** ("*I’ve never brought it up before*") instead of **validating her emotions** first. This made her feel **attacked**, not supported. --- ### **2. The Bipolar Factor: A Double-Edged Sword** Your girlfriend’s bipolar disorder **absolutely** affects how she processes criticism. People with bipolar disorder often: - **Shut down** when faced with perceived "pressure" (even if well-intentioned). - **Struggle with motivation** due to emotional dysregulation, making weight loss harder. - **React defensively** to any perceived "control" (even if you’re just suggesting changes). **What you could’ve done better:** - **Avoid framing it as a "failure."** Instead of *"you’ll never lose weight,"* try: - *"I know this is hard, but let’s celebrate small wins—like cutting out soda for a day!"* - *"Progress isn’t linear. Even if it’s slow, we’ll get there together."* - **Use "we" language consistently.** You said you wanted to do this as a team, but when she slipped up, you **shifted to "you" mode** ("*you’re not committed*"). - **Suggest professional help.** If she’s been struggling for a year, a **nutritionist or therapist** (especially one familiar with bipolar + weight issues) could offer **neutral, science-backed advice** without blame. --- ### **3. The Weight of the Weight (Literally and Figuratively)** Here’s the **hard truth**: Weight loss is **emotionally charged** for people with bipolar disorder (and many others) because: - **Food is often used as coping.** For someone with depression/bipolar, restricting food can feel like **another loss of control** (which is already a struggle). - **Body image is tied to self-worth.** If she’s been critical of herself for a year, **external pressure (even from you) can backfire** and trigger shame or avoidance. - **Rapid weight loss isn’t sustainable.** Even if she wanted to, **cutting out junk food cold turkey** could lead to bingeing later (a common bipolar-related pattern). **What you could’ve said instead:** > *"I know you’re frustrated, and I’m here for you. Let’s not focus on the scale right now—how about we just try replacing one junk food with something healthier this week? Even if it’s just swapping soda for sparkling water. No pressure, just baby steps."* --- ### **4. The Relationship Dynamic: Walking on Ice** You mentioned you **often back down in arguments** to avoid conflict. This is **healthy** in some ways (you’re avoiding unnecessary fights), but it can also: - **Create resentment** if she feels you’re **never assertive** (even when it’s needed). - **Reinforce passive behavior** in her—if she knows she can **shut down and win**, she might keep doing it. **How to balance this:** - **Pick your battles.** Weight loss is important to you, but **not worth a fight** if she’s not ready. Instead of pushing now, **plant the seed** for later. - **Set boundaries.** If she’s **constantly complaining** but not acting, you can say: > *"I love supporting you, but I can’t keep talking about this if you’re not ready to make changes. Let’s revisit this in a few months when you’re feeling more motivated."* - **Focus on health, not weight.** Instead of *"lose weight,"* try: - *"Let’s try a 30-day challenge to eat more veggies!"* - *"I’d love to go for walks with you—even just 10 minutes a day!"* --- ### **5. The Real Question: Are You the Asshole?** **No—but you’re not the hero either.** - **You’re not the asshole** because you’re **not demanding** or **shaming** her. You’re **genuinely concerned**. - **You’re not the hero** because **this isn’t your burden to carry alone**. Weight loss (or lack thereof) is **her responsibility**, and while you can **support her**, you can’t **fix her**. **The healthiest approach:** 1. **Stop framing it as a "weight loss" issue.** Instead, **focus on habits** (eating more veggies, moving more) that **incidentally** lead to weight loss. 2. **Avoid direct criticism.** If she’s eating junk food, **don’t call her out**—instead, **lead by example** (e.g., *"I’m trying to drink more water today—want to join me?"*). 3. **Give her space.** If she’s **defensive**, back off. If she’s **open**, suggest **small, non-threatening changes**. 4. **Protect your own mental health.** If this becomes a **constant source of conflict**, it’s okay to say: > *"I care about you, but I can’t keep having this conversation if it’s making you upset. Let’s talk about something else."* --- ### **Final Verdict: 0.3/1 (Not AITA, but Needs Adjustment)** You’re **not the bad guy**, but your **approach needs refinement** to avoid creating more tension. The key is: ✅ **Support her without enabling avoidance.** ✅ **Focus on habits, not weight.** ✅ **Protect your own emotional boundaries.** If she’s **truly committed**, she’ll engage. If not, **you can’t force her**—and that’s okay. The goal isn’t to "fix" her weight, but to **build a relationship where both of you feel heard and respected**. Would you like help drafting a **calmer way to bring this up next time**?
